Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

| order by files desc

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

TeamCity server (java) process spawning OS command shell — CVE-2026-63077 RCE execution AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-63077: the JetBrains TeamCity On-Premises server process (java/javaw running from a TeamCity install path) spawning a command interpreter or recon binary. The TeamCity *server* should almost never launch cmd/PowerShell/sh directly — build steps run on remote agents — so a shell child of the server JVM is a high-fidelity indicator of the unauthenticated agent-polling-protocol RCE executing OS commands with the server process's privileges. Rationale: Grounded in the JetBrains advisory statement that the flaw lets an attacker 'execute arbitrary operating system commands with the privileges of the TeamCity server process' via the agent polling protocol; the server JVM spawning a shell is the direct execution artefact. Cross-checked JetBrains advisory and IONIX/Rapid7-style analyses (CWE-502 deserialization in agent polling); no endpoint/IOC was disclosed so detection keys on the parent(java+TeamCity path)->child(shell) relationship rather than a URL. VCS binaries excluded to cut server-side git/svn noise. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/ • https://research.splunk.com/stories/jetbrains_teamcity_unauthenticated_rce/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Small/dev deployments where a TeamCity build agent is co-located on the server host and legitimately runs shell build steps under the same JVM tree
  • Administrator-run server-side maintenance or backup scripts invoked through TeamCity
  • Server-side VCS operations that shell out (git/svn/hg) — excluded in the query but variants may slip through
  • Health-check or monitoring plugins that spawn cmd/curl for self-tests
  • Custom TeamCity meta-runners configured to execute on the server rather than an agent
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("git.exe","svn.exe","hg.exe","mvn.cmd","gradle.bat") and ProcessCommandLine !has "HealthCheck" and not (DeviceName has_any ("agent","buildagent"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and confirm the parent JVM path is the TeamCity *server* (not an agent) and that the host's TeamCity version is below 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3 (or unpatched by the security-patch plugin). Recon commands (whoami/net/systeminfo) or download tooling (curl/certutil/bitsadmin) = strong true positive. 2) CONTAIN: Network-isolate the host, block untrusted inbound access to the TeamCity HTTP(S)/agent port, and rotate all credentials, tokens, and service-account secrets stored in TeamCity. 3) HUNT: Review TeamCity data dir and logs for new admin users/tokens, dropped webshells or plugins, and outbound connections from the JVM to public IPs; sweep other internet-facing TeamCity servers for the same parent->child pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("teamcity","jetbrains.buildServer","TeamCity") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "TeamCity"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami","id","curl","wget")
| where FileName !in~ ("git.exe","svn.exe","hg.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has "java" and ParentProcessName has "TeamCity"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\ipconfig.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamCity Server Process Spawning OS Command Shell (CVE-2026-63077)
id: 6f2a1c7e-4b90-4d55-8a3e-9c1f0b2e77aa
status: experimental
description: Detects the JetBrains TeamCity On-Premises server JVM (java/javaw from a TeamCity path) spawning a command interpreter or recon binary, the post-exploitation footprint of the CVE-2026-63077 unauthenticated agent-polling-protocol RCE.
references:
  - https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/
  - https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/28
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains: 'teamcity'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\javaw.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'

      - '\net.exe'
      - '\net1.exe'

      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'

falsepositives:
  - Co-located TeamCity build agent executing shell build steps on the server host
  - Server-side maintenance scripts launched by administrators
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\TeamCity\\* OR *\\teamcity\\*) @ParentImage:(*\\java.exe OR *\\javaw.exe OR *\\Java.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\Cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\nltest.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\curl.exe)

| ImageFileName!=/\\(git|svn|hg)\.exe$/i

Exposed / unpatched JetBrains TeamCity On-Premises vulnerable to CVE-2026-63077 AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces hosts running JetBrains TeamCity On-Premises that are flagged vulnerable to CVE-2026-63077 (CVSS 9.8), prioritising internet-facing instances that need immediate upgrade to 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3 or the security-patch plugin. This is an exposure/attack-surface hunt for the unauthenticated agent-polling-protocol RCE before it is weaponised. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-63077) and JetBrains-published fixed versions (2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3) from the article to enumerate vulnerable TeamCity On-Premises assets, weighting internet-facing exposure because the flaw needs only unauthenticated HTTP(S) access. Datadog/Falcon/Sigma/CloudWatch left empty — this is vulnerability-inventory (TVM) telemetry not carried by EDR process/network events, endpoint logs, or CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts patched via the JetBrains security-patch plugin (2017.1+) whose version string is unchanged and still reports as vulnerable in TVM
  • TeamCity build agents (not the server) flagged by software inventory but not exposing the vulnerable server endpoint
  • Decommissioned or offline TeamCity instances still in the asset inventory
  • Internal-only lab/dev TeamCity servers with no untrusted network path
  • Scanner version-detection error mapping a nightly/EAP build to the CVE
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a TeamCity *server* and check whether it is internet-facing (IsInternetFacing / PublicIP) and whether the security-patch plugin has been applied despite the version string. 2) CONTAIN: For any exposed unpatched server, restrict inbound access to the TeamCity HTTP(S)/agent-polling port to trusted agent IP ranges or place it behind VPN, then schedule the upgrade to 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3. 3) HUNT: On every flagged host, run the companion detection for the TeamCity server JVM spawning a shell and inspect TeamCity logs for suspicious agent-polling requests, newly created tokens, and unexpected admin accounts to rule out prior exploitation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-63077"
| join kind=leftouter (

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fileless memfd-backed binary executing as root (CVE-2026-53264 core-dump payload) AIInstallation High
Hunts the payoff stage of the STAR Labs CVE-2026-53264 traffic-control UAF LPE: the exploit copies itself into a memfd, overwrites core_pattern, and deliberately crashes a child so the kernel runs the memfd-backed binary as the root core-dump handler. This surfaces any process whose executable path resolves to an anonymous memfd descriptor while running as uid 0 (root) — a fileless, on-disk-less root execution that is extremely rare on production Linux. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact mechanic — 'places a copy of itself in a memfd ... run the memfd-backed binary as the root core-dump handler.' memfd path + uid 0 is the one point where this ROP-based exploit produces observable userland telemetry (the core_pattern overwrite happens in kernel memory via ROP, so no file-write event fires). Cross-checked against the Linux CNA CVE record. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-53264 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researcher-says-ai-helped-develop-linux.html
ATT&CKT1620 T1548 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container runtimes (runc, crun, podman, containerd-shim) exec'ing memfd-sealed binaries at container start
  • systemd or systemd-sysext running memfd-sealed / fd-passed units as root
  • Legitimate fileless deployment or self-protection tooling that memfd_create+execve
  • Security researchers detonating Linux LPE PoCs in a lab
  • Some JIT/interpreter runtimes that memfd-exec generated code
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("runc","crun","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","podman","systemd","systemd-sysext","dockerd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the host, capture the memfd process cmdline/uid/parent, dump memfd contents if resident, and read /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern — a memfd or pipe (|) handler plus a recent segfault/coredump in dmesg confirms the exploit chain. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the root memfd process, restore core_pattern to 'core', and set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 as a stopgap. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating account for prior unshare/user+net-namespace activity and clsact/flower tc setup, and sweep other hosts for the same memfd-as-root pattern plus unpatched kernels (CVE-2026-53264).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has "memfd:" or ProcessCommandLine has "memfd:"
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("runc","crun","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","podman","systemd","dockerd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "memfd" or ActingProcessName has "memfd" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "memfd:"
| where TargetUsername =~ "root" or ActorUsername =~ "root"
| where ParentProcessName !in~ ("runc","crun","containerd-shim","podman","systemd","dockerd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fileless memfd-Backed Process Executing as Root (CVE-2026-53264 Core-Dump Payload)
id: 8f3c2a1d-4e6b-4c9a-9b21-7a5d0f2e1c88
description: Detects a process whose executable image resolves to an anonymous memfd descriptor running as root, matching the CVE-2026-53264 traffic-control UAF LPE core-dump payload.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researcher-says-ai-helped-develop-linux.html
  - https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-53264

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_path="*memfd:*" OR Processes.process="*memfd:*") (Processes.user="root" OR Processes.user_id=0) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Unpatched kernels exposed to CVE-2026-53264 traffic-control UAF LPE AIReconnaissance High
Exposure/patch-management hunt for the public CVE-2026-53264 exploit. Surfaces assets whose kernel package is flagged vulnerable to the traffic-control (net/sched) use-after-free, so remediation can be prioritised — the article stresses installing a distro kernel carrying the fix rather than trusting the upstream version number (fixed builds: 5.10.259, 5.15.210, 6.1.176, 6.6.143, 6.12.94, 6.18.36, 7.0.13; mainline 7.1-rc7). Rationale: Keyed on the article's single concrete IOC — the CVE id CVE-2026-53264 — plus its explicit list of fixed kernel builds, making this a clean, deployable prioritisation hunt against vulnerability-management telemetry. Note TVM package status does not confirm the required unprivileged-userns + CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT/CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER preconditions, so treat hits as candidate exposure, not confirmed exploitability. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-53264 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researcher-says-ai-helped-develop-linux.html
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts flagged vulnerable by package version but with unprivileged user namespaces disabled (kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0) — not exploitable
  • Kernels lacking CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT or CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER — the demonstrated chain does not apply
  • TVM lag showing a host as vulnerable shortly after a live-patched/kexec kernel update
  • Distros that backported the fix without bumping the upstream version string, causing version-only scanners to misreport
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm each flagged host's running kernel (uname -r) against the fixed builds and check whether unprivileged user namespaces are enabled (sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone) and whether CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT/CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER are compiled in — all three are required for the public exploit. 2) Contain: for exploitable hosts, schedule the distro kernel update carrying the fix; as interim mitigation set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0. 3) Hunt: on any exposed host, run the memfd-root detection (UC1) retrospectively to check for prior exploitation before patching.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
NightLedger DLL side-load: AppVShNotify.exe loading co-located SspiCli.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts Mirage Kitten's NightLedger backdoor, which masquerades as SspiCli.dll and is loaded via delay-load/search-order hijacking by a legitimate AppVShNotify.exe placed in a writable directory. Fires when AppVShNotify.exe loads SspiCli.dll from anywhere other than the Windows system directories, which is anomalous because the genuine SspiCli.dll only ships under System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact side-load pair (legitimate AppVShNotify.exe + malicious SspiCli.dll masquerade) plus the location anomaly (genuine SspiCli.dll only ships in System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS) and the sample MD5 c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac. Corroborated as UNC1549/Nimbus Manticore's signature low-level DLL side-loading tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/suspected-iranian-unc1549-targets-israel-middle-east • https://socprime.com/active-threats/detecting-nimbus-manticore-and-their-sideloading-infection-chains/ • https://www.nextron-systems.com/2026/06/01/detecting-nimbus-manticore-and-their-sideloading-infection-chains/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1574.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine App-V AppVShNotify.exe loading SspiCli.dll from System32 (already excluded by the path filter)
  • Third-party installer temporarily extracting AppVShNotify.exe alongside Office redistributables into a staging/temp dir
  • EDR/AV quarantine or backup tooling copying the pair into a non-standard restore path
  • Developer/test machines running App-V components from a custom install root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Office" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft Application Virtualization\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the LoadedDllPath and hash the SspiCli.dll at that location; a hash not matching the Microsoft-signed System32 copy (or matching c832ecd1...) is a confirmed side-load. Confirm AppVShNotify.exe sits in a user-writable directory. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the AppVShNotify.exe process tree, and quarantine the co-located SspiCli.dll. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for the mutex-guarded beacon to realhealthshop.com/tjconsultingservices.com and reads of C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log; sweep the fleet for AppVShNotify.exe outside Office/App-V paths.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AppVShNotify.exe"
| where FileName =~ "SspiCli.dll"
| where not (FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" or FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" or FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS")
   or MD5 =~ "c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedDllPath = FolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceImageLoadEvents

| where not (FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" or FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" or FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS")
   or MD5 =~ "c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedDllPath = FolderPath, SHA256, MD5

NightLedger C2 beacon to Mirage Kitten realhealthshop / tjconsultingservices domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts NightLedger's HTTPS command-and-control by resolving/connecting to the group's hardcoded primary and fallback C2 domains and adjacent IOC infrastructure. High-fidelity because these are dedicated Mirage Kitten C2 domains with no legitimate business use. Rationale: Uses the article's hardcoded primary C2 (realhealthshop[.]com), fallback (tjconsultingservices[.]com), IOC-list domains (businessmixture[.]com, aecert[.]org), and the highly distinctive NightLedger URI endpoints (/edfcvfgbhnjmkqwasderfgg, /qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj, /wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt) which are random strings with zero benign collision risk. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/suspected-iranian-unc1549-targets-israel-middle-east • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/actor/unc1549
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/sandbox detonation of the sample from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel enrichment or web-proxy pre-fetch tooling resolving IOC domains for reputation lookups
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance itself logging the query before blocking
  • Analyst manually browsing the C2 domain during triage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName making the connection - AppVShNotify.exe or rundll32.exe from a user-writable path confirms NightLedger; a browser resolving it may be benign research. 2) Contain: block the four domains and the NightLedger URI paths at proxy/DNS, isolate any host with a non-browser process reaching them. 3) Hunt: correlate to the AppVShNotify/SspiCli side-load on the same host, pull the beacon interval, and search for the POST-based exfil endpoints /qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj and /wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("realhealthshop.com","tjconsultingservices.com","businessmixture.com","aecert.org")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("/edfcvfgbhnjmkqwasderfgg","/qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj","/wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("realhealthshop.com","tjconsultingservices.com","businessmixture.com","aecert.org")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BridgeHead/ArcBridge WebSocket tunneler egress to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Mirage Kitten's ArcBridge/BridgeHead WebSocket SOCKS5 tunnelers, which establish an HTTPS WebSocket to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net /connect and relay operator traffic through the victim. Distinctive because the dedicated Azure Web App subdomain is attacker-controlled relay infrastructure, unlike generic azurewebsites.net app traffic. Rationale: Anchored on the exact tunneler relay host (smartconnect.azurewebsites.net /connect WebSocket) named in the article's captured request. Azure C2 fronting is corroborated as UNC1549's documented technique; the Defender query surfaces the initiating process so an analyst can confirm it is the sideloaded DLL host (e.g. rundll32/unusual path) rather than a legitimate app. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/suspected-iranian-unc1549-targets-israel-middle-east • https://socprime.com/active-threats/detecting-nimbus-manticore-and-their-sideloading-infection-chains/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-owned Azure Web App that a customer coincidentally named 'smartconnect' (verify tenant ownership of the app)
  • Security sandbox detonation reaching the relay host
  • Proxy/CASB inspection appliance re-resolving the host
  • Vendor SmartConnect-branded SaaS product using a similarly named Azure endpoint (validate exact FQDN and initiating process)
Response runbook
1) Triage: check InitiatingProcessFileName/Path - a DLL host under %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\VisualStudio or univpn\promote, or rundll32 spawning the connection, confirms the tunneler; note sustained/backoff connection cadence. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block smartconnect.azurewebsites.net at the proxy, and capture the loaded module (unbcl.dll / libwinpthread-1.dll). 3) Hunt: pivot to internal SOCKS-relayed connections originating from the victim, review lateral TCP flows sourced from that host, and sweep for the same DLL names fleet-wide.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort)
         by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery endswith "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BridgeHead/ArcBridge tunneler DLL dropped as unbcl.dll / libwinpthread-1.dll in anomalous paths AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the on-disk staging of Mirage Kitten's WebSocket tunnelers, written as unbcl.dll under %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\VisualStudio or as libwinpthread-1.dll under C:\program files (x86)\univpn\promote. Detects the file-write of these specific DLL names into these specific sideload-host directories. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact tunneler-on-disk artifacts: unbcl.dll in %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\VisualStudio and libwinpthread-1.dll in C:\program files (x86)\univpn\promote. Both are legitimate-looking DLL names, so the fidelity comes from pairing each name with its specific abused host directory rather than the name alone. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/mirage-kitten-new-tools/120811/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/detecting-nimbus-manticore-and-their-sideloading-infection-chains/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate UniVPN client install/update writing libwinpthread-1.dll into its own univpn\promote directory (verify signer and hash)
  • A MinGW-built application legitimately bundling libwinpthread-1.dll if installed under a matching path
  • Visual Studio extension/component writing an unbcl.dll into the VisualStudio local-appdata folder
  • Backup/restore or migration tooling copying an existing DLL tree into these paths
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("univpninstaller.exe","univpn.exe") and FolderPath has @"\univpn\promote\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped DLL and check the Authenticode signer; an unsigned or unknown-hash unbcl.dll/libwinpthread-1.dll in these paths is high-suspicion. Identify InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote it. 2) Contain: quarantine the DLL, isolate the host, and look for the sideload-host EXE that would load it. 3) Hunt: check for outbound WebSocket to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net from that host, review the GetUserNameA-based username gate behavior, and sweep both DLL names across the fleet joined to their abused directories.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("unbcl.dll","libwinpthread-1.dll")
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\VisualStudio\" or FolderPath has @"\univpn\promote\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("unbcl.dll","libwinpthread-1.dll")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\VisualStudio\" or TargetFilePath has @"\univpn\promote\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\(unbcl\.dll|libwinpthread-1\.dll)$/i

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("realhealthshop.com", "tjconsultingservices.com", "businessmixture.com", "aecert.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or SHA1 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or MD5 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or SHA1 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or MD5 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attackers Exploit Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator Command Injection Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A maximum-severity security flaw impacting on-premises versions of Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) has come under active exploitation in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-16812 (CVSS score: 10.0), is a case of operating system command injection that could pave the way for arbitrary code execution. Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Inbound access to VeloCloud Orchestrator from Arista-published CVE-2026-16812 attacker IPs · [LLM] OS command-injection payload in VeloCloud Orchestrator web requests (CVE-2026-16812) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound egress from VeloCloud Orchestrator host to CVE-2026-16812 attacker IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Inbound access to VeloCloud Orchestrator from Arista-published CVE-2026-16812 attacker IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound connections to the on-prem VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) web interface originating from the three source IPs Arista attributed to active CVE-2026-16812 command-injection exploitation. First-order IOC match on the exploitation source infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the three attacker source IPs Arista published as CVE-2026-16812 IOCs (corroborated by CISA KEV and BleepingComputer). Exact-IP source match against an internet-facing orchestrator is inherently low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/27/cisa-adds-two-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/arista-patches-velocloud-orchestrator-zero-day-exploited-in-attacks/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or vulnerability-scanning vendor that legitimately owns/reuses one of the published IP ranges probing your perimeter
  • A shared-hosting/CDN IP that Arista listed being reused for benign traffic (advisory notes the list is not definitive)
  • Internal security team replaying the attacker IP during authorized validation testing
  • Security appliance sinkhole/honeypot deliberately soliciting the IPs
  • NAT egress collision where an unrelated internal service shares the same public IP as an attacker
Suppression filter
| where DestinationPort in (443, 8443, 80)  // scope to VCO web interface ports; drop unrelated services sharing perimeter NAT
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the DestinationIP is a VCO host and inspect the matching web/WAF logs for the request path, body and HTTP response code around the connection time. 2) Contain: Block the three IPs at the perimeter, restrict the VCO web interface to trusted admin networks, and snapshot VCO web/app/system/DB logs and filesystem timestamps before remediation per Arista guidance. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the VCO host for outbound connections to these IPs, unexpected admin account changes, new/edited config or scripts, and lateral access toward managed VeloCloud Edge devices; rotate VCO and Edge credentials if compromise confirmed.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

OS command-injection payload in VeloCloud Orchestrator web requests (CVE-2026-16812) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-16812 exploitation by inspecting inbound HTTP requests to the VeloCloud Orchestrator web interface for shell metacharacters and command-execution primitives (semicolons, pipes, subshell/backtick syntax, download utilities) in the URL/query — the signature of the unauthenticated OS command-injection (CWE-78) being weaponized. Rationale: Targets the article's core attack (unauthenticated OS command injection, CWE-78 per Arista/CISA) by matching shell metacharacters and command primitives in VCO web requests, with an attacker-IP boost flag from the published IOCs to rank true positives. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://securityaffairs.com/196130/security/u-s-cisa-adds-arista-velocloud-orchestrator-and-fortinet-fortios-flaws-to-its-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate VCO API calls that carry pipes or semicolons in query strings (filter expressions, base64 blobs ending in padding)
  • Administrative automation/scripts posting config payloads containing shell-like characters
  • URL-encoded JSON bodies where '%7C'/'%3B' appear inside legitimate values
  • Security scanners (Nessus/Qualys) firing benign command-injection probes during authorized scans
  • Browsers submitting search or filter fields containing '&&' or backticks
Suppression filter
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","GET","PUT") and (FromKnownAttacker or RequestURL has_any ("$(","`","/bin/","curl ","wget "))  // require a strong command primitive or attacker-IP context to cut benign pipe/semicolon noise
Response runbook
1) Triage: Prioritize hits where FromKnownAttacker==true, then read the full RequestURL/body and the VCO response code/size to judge whether the injected command executed. 2) Contain: If execution is evident (200 with anomalous body, or follow-on egress), isolate the VCO web interface to trusted networks and preserve web/app/system/DB logs before patching to the fixed VCO release (5.2.3.14 / 6.1.3.4 / 6.4.2.4 / 7.0.0.1). 3) Hunt: Search the VCO host for spawned shells, new files under config/script directories, outbound connections to the attacker IPs, and unexpected admin-activity or credential changes reaching managed Edge devices.
let AttackerIPs = dynamic(["8.19.75.217","206.72.242.124","206.72.242.162"]);
let CmdInjectTokens = dynamic([";","|","$(","`","%3B","%7C","%24%28","%60","&&","/bin/","curl ","wget "," nc "]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has_any (CmdInjectTokens)
| extend FromKnownAttacker = SourceIP in (AttackerIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, FromKnownAttacker, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by FromKnownAttacker desc, TimeGenerated desc

Outbound egress from VeloCloud Orchestrator host to CVE-2026-16812 attacker IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the VCO host (or any internal host) initiating outbound connections to the three Arista-published attacker IPs — a post-exploitation signal (reverse shell / C2 / data staging) that Arista explicitly told operators to watch for as 'unexpected outbound network activity from the VCO host.' Rationale: Directly operationalizes Arista's guidance to monitor 'unexpected outbound network activity from the VCO host' using the three published IOC IPs as egress destinations — a compromise confirmation distinct from the inbound-access pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/arista-patches-velocloud-orchestrator-zero-day-exploited-in-attacks/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An analyst or scanner deliberately connecting to the attacker IPs during authorized validation
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling that resolves/pings IOC IPs automatically
  • One of the published IPs later being reassigned to a benign SaaS/CDN endpoint an internal host legitimately uses
  • Proxy/VPN egress where the destination IP is shared infrastructure
  • Backup or telemetry service coincidentally hosted on the same netblock
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP != ""  // retain source attribution; suppress known sanctioned scanner source IPs here, e.g. and SourceIP !in ("10.10.10.10")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify SourceIP — if it is the VCO host, treat as confirmed compromise; review the initiating process/command line and byte volume to distinguish beacon vs bulk exfil. 2) Contain: Block egress to the three IPs, network-isolate the VCO host, and preserve VCO app/system/DB logs and file timestamps before rebuilding from a trusted image per Arista guidance. 3) Hunt: Rotate VCO and managed Edge-device credentials, validate managed-device state for tampering, and search other internal hosts for connections to the same IPs to scope lateral movement.
let AttackerIPs = dynamic(["8.19.75.217","206.72.242.124","206.72.242.162"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (AttackerIPs)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionRequest")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count() by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
let AttackerIPs = dynamic(["8.19.75.217","206.72.242.124","206.72.242.162"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in (AttackerIPs)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Bytes=sum(SentBytes), Conns=count() by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol
| order by Bytes desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
