Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'

            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound FastJson @type payload with jar:/ldap:/rmi: reference to Spring Boot app (CVE-2026-16723)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Spring Boot Java fat-JAR spawning shell/recon child process (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 RCE) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers target US firms in FastJson RCE zero-day attacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Java application making outbound LDAP/RMI connection (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 remote class load)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Inbound FastJson @type payload with jar:/ldap:/rmi: reference to Spring Boot app (CVE-2026-16723) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP request bodies/URIs carrying a FastJson '@type' key alongside a nested jar:, ldap:, rmi: URL or JdbcRowSetImpl/dataSourceName reference — the exploitation shape for CVE-2026-16723 against internet-facing Spring Boot fat-JAR apps. Article-specific because it keys on the @type + remote-resource-lookup combination, not generic deserialization. Rationale: Keys on the CVE-2026-16723 exploitation signature — a FastJson '@type' key co-occurring with a jar:/ldap:/rmi: remote-resource URL or the JdbcRowSetImpl/dataSourceName lookup class — confirmed by Imperva's advisory and the public jsontype RCE lab. Only expressible on WAF/proxy telemetry that captures request bodies; endpoint EDR/FDR do not ship HTTP bodies, hence Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.imperva.com/blog/imperva-customers-protected-against-cve-2026-16723-critical-fastjson-1-x-zero-day-rce/ • https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83 • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, Nessus, Nuclei) probing for fastjson with @type test payloads
  • Legitimate APIs that accept a client-supplied field literally named 'type' where the value contains a jar: or ldap: URI
  • Internal red-team / BAS (Picus, SafeBreach) exercises replaying deserialization payloads
  • Log-shipping of stored @type strings in JSON documents that are echoed back into request URLs
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has_any ("nuclei","nessus") or Message has_any ("nuclei","nessus") or SourceIP in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request from the WAF/proxy for the matched SourceIP; confirm the body contains @type plus a remote jar:/ldap:/rmi: URL and identify the DestinationHostName Spring Boot app and its FastJson version (1.2.68-1.2.83?). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, enable FastJson SafeMode (-Dfastjson.parser.safeMode=true) on the target app, and isolate the app host if outbound class-load already occurred. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'Java outbound LDAP/RMI' and 'Java fat-JAR spawning shell' on the destination host within a 5-minute window of the request to confirm code execution.

     or Message has_any ("jar:","ldap:","rmi:","dataSourceName","JdbcRowSetImpl")

Spring Boot Java fat-JAR spawning shell/recon child process (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects a Java process launched as a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar xxx.jar) spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash or a recon binary — the post-exploitation payload of CVE-2026-16723 landing on the app server. Article-specific: it requires the '-jar' parent context Alibaba names as the sole deployment prerequisite. Rationale: Anchors on Alibaba's stated prerequisite — a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar xxx.jar) — as the parent, paired with a shell/recon child, which is the concrete RCE outcome of CVE-2026-16723. Parent+child pairing keeps FP low versus a bare java or bare powershell query. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fastjson-1x-rce-vulnerability-targeted.html • https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83 • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab
ATT&CKT1190 T1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Jenkins/GitLab/TeamCity build agents (Java) legitimately invoking sh/bash/cmd for build steps
  • Java-based application servers shelling out to certutil/curl for cert or health-check tasks
  • Elastic/Logstash Java agents spawning helper processes
  • Admins running gradlew/mvnw wrappers that fork shells from a java parent
  • Monitoring tooling (Java) calling nslookup/ping for connectivity checks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jenkins","gitlab-runner","teamcity","elastic-agent","logstash") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gradlew","mvnw"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitiatingProcessCommandLine to confirm the fat-jar name and whether the child cmdline shows recon/download (whoami, curl to external IP); correlate with any inbound @type WAF hit on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the app server, kill the java parent, and apply FastJson SafeMode or migrate to fastjson2 (no vendor patch exists). 3) Hunt: on the same host review DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound LDAP/RMI (UC below) and any dropped .class/.jar in temp, and sweep the fleet for the same fat-jar name running vulnerable FastJson 1.2.68-1.2.83.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","whoami","net.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe","ping.exe","id","uname")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","/java")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","/sh","/bash","/dash","whoami","net.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Spring Boot Java Fat-JAR Spawning Shell or Recon Process (FastJson CVE-2026-16723)
id: 3f8c1e2a-7b4d-4a91-9c6e-2f1a8d5b0c33
status: experimental
description: Detects a Java process launched as a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar) spawning a shell or reconnaissance binary, consistent with RCE via FastJson CVE-2026-16723.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-target-us-firms-in-fastjson-rce-zero-day-attacks/
  - https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/28
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1059
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\javaw.exe'
      - '/java'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '-jar'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '\whoami.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\nslookup.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
  - CI/CD agents (Jenkins, GitLab runner) that legitimately shell out from a Java runner
  - Java application servers invoking system utilities for housekeeping
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\java.exe OR *\\javaw.exe OR *\\Java.exe) @ParentCommandLine:*-jar* @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\nslookup.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^javaw?\.exe$|^java$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|net|whoami|certutil|bitsadmin|nslookup|curl|wget)\.exe$|\/(sh|bash|dash|whoami|curl|wget|id|uname)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java") AND Processes.parent_process="*-jar*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","net.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe","ping.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Java application making outbound LDAP/RMI connection (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 remote class load) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects a java -jar process initiating an outbound connection to LDAP (389/636), RMI registry (1099) or the JNDI-exploit-kit LDAP port (1389) on a public host — the attacker-controlled resource lookup FastJson performs before AutoType checks, pulling a malicious class. Article-specific: ties the egress to a Spring Boot fat-JAR process on JNDI/RMI ports. Rationale: Corroborated detection indicator from Imperva/the PoC lab: outbound LDAP/RMI from an app server to an unexpected external host is the JNDI/defineClass remote class-load step. Scoping to a java -jar process on JNDI/RMI ports keeps this high-fidelity; a directory-bound corporate LDAP server is normally internal, not public. Cross-checked against: • https://www.imperva.com/blog/imperva-customers-protected-against-cve-2026-16723-critical-fastjson-1-x-zero-day-rce/ • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab • https://medium.com/@pa2sw0rd/deep-dive-into-fastjson-deserialization-vulnerabilities-from-principles-to-practical-defense-c3be134ec8a6
ATT&CKT1105 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java app authenticating users against an external/cloud-hosted LDAP directory (e.g. some managed AD/LDAP)
  • Java RMI microservices calling a partner RMI registry over 1099
  • Legacy apps configured with a public LDAP endpoint for address-book lookups
  • Vulnerability scanners generating JNDI callbacks during authorized testing
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP != "" and not (RemoteIP startswith "10." or RemoteIP startswith "192.168." or RemoteIP matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP — is it a known corporate/cloud LDAP or an unfamiliar external host/VPS? Check the fat-jar name and whether a shell child spawned on the same host within seconds. 2) Contain: block egress to the RemoteIP on JNDI/RMI ports from server subnets, isolate the host, and enable FastJson SafeMode on the app. 3) Hunt: capture any class file the JVM fetched, pivot to process-tree UC for java-spawned shells, and enumerate other hosts running FastJson 1.2.68-1.2.83 fat-jars that egressed to the same IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (389, 636, 1099, 1389)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActionType has "Connection"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where RemotePort in (389, 636, 1099, 1389)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound connection from known CVE-2026-16812 exploitation IPs to VCO web interface
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] VeloCloud Orchestrator web service spawning shell for DB export / archive / egress (CVE-2026-16812)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Unexpected outbound egress from VeloCloud Orchestrator host (C2 / data exfil)
Inbound connection from known CVE-2026-16812 exploitation IPs to VCO web interface AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound TCP/HTTP(S) connections to the VeloCloud Orchestrator management interface originating from the three IP addresses Arista attributed to active exploitation of the unauthenticated command-injection zero-day. Any hit is a direct IOC match against confirmed attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the three exploitation IPs published in the Arista advisory (verbatim in SA-0144 and CISA KEV) — a direct infrastructure IOC match with no behavioural inference required. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanner or CTI provider that happens to reuse one of these IPs for benign scanning (rare, verify with reverse DNS)
  • Shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a legitimate service after Arista's observation window
  • Internal red-team sourcing from an IP that collides with the IOC set
  • Threat-intel platform test/heartbeat traffic replaying IOC lists
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a VCO management host and pull the corresponding web access log lines for the source IP — look for encoded chars / internal-service path components around the connection time. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at the perimeter, restrict the VCO web interface to admin networks only, and snapshot logs + filesystem timestamps before any remediation. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same VCO host for web-service→shell process spawns (UC2) and unexpected outbound egress (UC3); if confirmed, treat the appliance as compromised — patch is insufficient, rotate all credentials/certs/keys and validate managed Edge devices.

VeloCloud Orchestrator web service spawning shell for DB export / archive / egress (CVE-2026-16812) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation signature of the VCO OS command-injection flaw: the orchestrator's web tier (nginx/Node.js/Java) spawning a Unix shell or data-handling tool that runs a database dump, archive creation, or outbound fetch. Directly targets Arista's 'unexpected command execution, file creation, database exports, or archive files' IOC guidance. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CWE-78 exploitation outcome Arista called out (unexpected command execution, database export, archive files) by requiring a web-tier parent process spawning a shell/dump/archive/egress tool — a combination that essentially never occurs on a healthy orchestrator appliance. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled DB backup job legitimately invoking mysqldump/pg_dump under a web-service account (verify cron/systemd-timer parentage, not a web-request-driven spawn)
  • Appliance health/telemetry scripts calling curl/wget to Arista update endpoints
  • Vendor support engineer running diagnostic tar/gzip during a maintenance session
  • In-product config-export feature shelling out to tar (validate against expected admin action)
  • Node.js app legitimately spawning sh for a documented internal maintenance task
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("cron","crond","systemd","systemd-cron") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "/etc/cron"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and command line — confirm the parent is the web-facing service and whether the shell ran a DB dump, archive, or egress; correlate the timestamp with inbound web requests (UC1) and access-log anomalies. 2) Contain: isolate the VCO host from the network, kill the offending process, and preserve logs + filesystem timestamps before remediation. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written/archived and any outbound transfers (UC3); if a dump/archive left the host, assume compromise of managed device inventories, credentials, certs and keys — rotate everything and validate/replace the appliance rather than relying on the patch alone.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nginx","node","httpd","apache2","java","gunicorn","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","mysqldump","pg_dump","pg_dumpall","tar","zip","gzip","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mysqldump","pg_dump","tar ","zip ","gzip","curl ","wget ","/dev/tcp/","base64","nc ","ncat ")
    or FileName in~ ("mysqldump","pg_dump","pg_dumpall","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux" or isempty(DvcOs)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("nginx","node","httpd","apache2","java","gunicorn","python")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","mysqldump","pg_dump","pg_dumpall","tar","zip","gzip","curl","wget","/nc","ncat")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("mysqldump","pg_dump","tar ","zip ","gzip","curl ","wget ","/dev/tcp/","base64","nc ","ncat ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unexpected outbound egress from VeloCloud Orchestrator host (C2 / data exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound HTTP(S)/TCP initiated by the VCO host — either back to the three known exploitation IPs, or by a web-service/shell process reaching a public address. An orchestrator normally receives management connections, so service-account egress to the internet indicates reverse-shell C2 or exfil of the exported database/archive. Rationale: Combines Arista's 'unexpected outbound HTTP/HTTPS from the VCO host' guidance with the three attributed IPs and a service/shell-process egress filter, so the detection fires on reverse-shell C2 or exfil of the dumped DB even when the destination differs from the published IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VCO reaching Arista/VMware update, licensing, or telemetry endpoints over HTTPS (baseline and allowlist the legitimate FQDNs)
  • NTP/DNS or monitoring-agent egress from the appliance to approved public resolvers
  • Node.js app calling an approved external API (e.g. cloud object storage for legitimate backups)
  • Package-manager (apt/yum) update traffic during a maintenance window
  • Proxy/NAT collapsing many hosts onto the VCO source IP inflating the egress picture
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "arista.com" and RemoteUrl !has "velocloud.net" and RemoteUrl !has "vmware.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the egress destination and the initiating process/command line — is it a known Arista endpoint or an unfamiliar public IP; check bytes-out for bulk transfer consistent with a DB/archive exfil. 2) Contain: block the destination and the three IOC IPs, cut the appliance's outbound internet path, and capture a memory/disk snapshot before remediation. 3) Hunt: tie the egress back to a web-service→shell spawn (UC2) and inbound exploit-IP hits (UC1) to confirm the full chain; if exfil is confirmed, rotate all VCO-managed credentials, certificates and cryptographic keys and validate every managed Edge device for tampering.

Dysphoria IoT botnet blockchain (ENS/SNS) C2 name resolution AICommand & Control High
Hunts hosts resolving the Dysphoria botnet's blockchain name-service C2 records (m3rnbvs5d.eth, burrberry.eth, 24carnforth2merseyside.sol) or ENS/SNS-over-DNS gateways. Enterprise endpoints and IoT gear have no legitimate reason to resolve .eth/.sol names, making this the highest-fidelity pivot on the article's headline blockchain-C2 innovation. Rationale: Uses the three ENS/SNS C2 domains confirmed by gbhackers and BleepingComputer plus common ENS-over-DNS gateways (.eth.link/.eth.limo). A resolution of any .eth/.sol name from enterprise or IoT telemetry is inherently anomalous, so this fires on the article's core blockchain-C2 behaviour with minimal noise. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1568 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstation running a web3/ethers.js or Solana SDK project resolving .eth/.sol names
  • Browser extension (MetaMask, Brave crypto wallet) resolving ENS names for a user
  • Blockchain node or NFT tooling deliberately installed on a lab host
  • Security researcher detonating unrelated crypto malware in a sandbox that reports to the same tenant
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("metamask.exe","brave.exe","chrome.exe") and DeviceName has_any ("DEV-","LAB-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and process — a router/camera/IoT device or a server (not a dev laptop with a wallet) resolving .eth/.sol is high-confidence malicious. Check whether the same host also hit the distribution-node IPs (UC2). 2) Contain: isolate the device from the network; for managed hosts kill the process and block the resolved IPs at the egress firewall. IoT gear should be power-cycled and firmware-reflashed as it cannot be cleaned in place. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IPs across all egress logs, look for weak-Telnet/SSH logons (UC4) and UPnP relay behaviour (UC6) on the same subnet to scope the botnet foothold.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
    or RemoteUrl endswith ".eth" or RemoteUrl endswith ".sol"
    or RemoteUrl has_any (".eth.link",".eth.limo",".sol.link")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
    or Name endswith ".eth" or Name endswith ".sol"
    or Name endswith ".eth.link" or Name endswith ".eth.limo"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Queries=make_set(Name,10)
    by Computer, ClientIP
| order by LastSeen desc

Callout to Dysphoria distribution-node IPv4 addresses AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts when any monitored host or firewall-observed client connects to the five Dysphoria distribution-node IPs decoded from the burrberry.eth ENS record. These endpoints are infected relays that serve the current server list over HTTP; a connection to them indicates a bot fetching C2 infrastructure. Rationale: Five hard IPv4 IOCs from the article's decoded burrberry.eth record. Direct IP-match detection is deployable across any egress log source; flagged Medium confidence because the IPs appear only in the original THN IOC set and were not independently confirmed by the two corroborating write-ups, so hits should be validated against UC1/UC4 context. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared hosting / VPS provider re-assigns one of these IPs to a benign service after botnet takedown
  • Threat-intel scanner or sandbox in the environment deliberately probing the IOC IPs
  • Security vendor sinkhole now occupying the address space
  • Corporate proxy aggregating traffic makes attribution to the true source host ambiguous
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connecting host and initiating process; a bot typically fetches an HTTP server list, so look for outbound HTTP/GET to these IPs. Cross-check the same host for .eth/.sol resolution (UC1). 2) Contain: block all five IPs at the perimeter, isolate the source host, and capture the process command line before killing it. 3) Hunt: enumerate every internal host that touched these IPs, then hunt those hosts for inbound Telnet/SSH brute-force (UC4) and relay behaviour (UC6) to map botnet spread.

    by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by LastSeen desc

IoT/server host contacting public blockchain RPC or ENS/SNS gateways AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoints and IoT-adjacent hosts that reach public Ethereum/Solana RPC providers or ENS/SNS resolution gateways. Dysphoria resolves C2 through blockchain name services, which requires reaching an RPC endpoint or gateway; a device with no crypto use-case doing this is a blockchain-C2 beacon candidate. Rationale: Grounded in the article's ENS/SNS resolution model (confirmed by XLab/gbhackers): resolving blockchain names requires an RPC or gateway hop. Scoped to the common public providers so it surfaces the resolution channel; kept hunting/Medium because legitimate crypto tooling shares these hosts, so it must be triaged by host role. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/dysphoria-iot-botnet-adds-blockchain-c2.html
ATT&CKT1102 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/data teams running dApp or NFT backends against Infura/Alchemy/Ankr
  • Corporate treasury or finance host using a legitimate crypto custody service
  • Browser wallet extensions on user laptops
  • CI/CD runner building a web3 project pulling RPC endpoints
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("DEV","LAB","BUILD") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: filter to hosts whose role has no crypto justification (routers, cameras, print servers, generic app servers). Confirm the initiating process — a non-browser, non-node binary is suspicious. 2) Contain: for confirmed non-legitimate hosts, isolate and block the RPC domains at egress; validate against UC1 (.eth/.sol resolution) on the same host. 3) Hunt: review whether the host subsequently connected to the distribution IPs (UC2) or began relaying (UC6); scope to the whole IoT VLAN.

Telnet/SSH weak-credential brute-force into edge/IoT devices (Dysphoria re-infection) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the article's primary propagation vector post-JackSkid: repeated Telnet (23) / SSH (22) auth failures from an external source followed by a successful logon on the same device. This is the initial-access step that re-seeds the botnet after infrastructure disruption. Rationale: Article and both corroborating sources state weak Telnet/SSH credentials remain 'the most consistent way in.' The failure-burst-then-success correlation on ports 22/23 targets the exact re-infection primitive rather than generic auth noise; thresholds are commented for tuning. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1078.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated config-management (Ansible/rsync) that mistypes credentials during a rollout
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) performing credentialed SSH checks
  • Legitimate admin fat-fingering a password several times before success
  • Backup/monitoring agent with an expired key retrying then succeeding after rotation
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0/8") and TargetUsername !in~ ("ansible","svc-backup","nessus","qualys")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and the target is an edge/IoT device; check geolocation and whether the successful account is a default (admin/root/guest). 2) Contain: block the source IP, force-rotate the device credentials, and disable remote management/Telnet per the article's guidance. 3) Hunt: on the compromised device, look for immediate outbound to distribution IPs (UC2) or .eth/.sol resolution (UC1); sweep the subnet for the same source IP hitting other devices.
let Failed = DeviceLogonEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
    | where RemotePort in (22, 23)
    | summarize FailCount=count() by DeviceName, RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
    | where FailCount > 20;   // >20 failed edge-device logons/hr = guessing
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where RemotePort in (22, 23)
| join kind=inner Failed on DeviceName, RemoteIP
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, AccountName, RemotePort, FailCount
| order by Timestamp desc
let Failed = ImAuthentication
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventResult == "Failure"
    | where LogonProtocol in~ ("ssh","telnet") or TargetAppName in~ ("sshd","telnetd")
    | summarize FailCount=count() by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
    | where FailCount > 20;   // >20 failures/hr from one source = guessing
ImAuthentication
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventResult == "Success"
| where LogonProtocol in~ ("ssh","telnet")
| join kind=inner Failed on DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, TargetUsername, FailCount
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(linux.syslog OR linux.auditd) @process.name:(sshd OR telnetd OR telnet) @evt.outcome:failure
APPLICATION

| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("ssh","sshd","telnet","telnetd") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")`
| where count > 20
| join type=inner src dest [| tstats `summariesonly` count as success_count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("ssh","sshd","telnet","telnetd") Authentication.action=success by Authentication.src Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")`]
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("ssh","sshd","telnet","telnetd") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")`
| where count > 20
| join type=inner src dest [| tstats summariesonly=false count as success_count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("ssh","sshd","telnet","telnetd") Authentication.action=success by Authentication.src Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")`]
| sort - count
CVE-2025-9528 Linksys E1700 /goform/systemCommand command injection AIExploitation High
Detects exploitation of CVE-2025-9528, a Linksys E1700 command-injection flaw named in both the XLab and CNCERT lists as a Dysphoria propagation vector. Fires on inbound HTTP requests to /goform/systemCommand carrying the injectable command parameter. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoint (/goform/systemCommand) and injectable parameter (command=) confirmed by NVD and the GitHub advisory GHSA-3m47-gr9p-qrv3, combined with common IoT-loader payload tokens (wget/curl/tftp/busybox/chmod, shell metacharacters). The path is unique enough that any hit is high-fidelity exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-9528 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3m47-gr9p-qrv3
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scan (Nessus/Nuclei) firing the public PoC against inventory
  • Internal red-team validating the patch
  • Security researcher replaying the disclosed exploit in a lab
  • Legitimate Linksys admin script that coincidentally posts to the same goform endpoint (rare)
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8","192.168.0.0/16") and Host !has_any ("scanner","nessus","redteam")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target is an internet-facing Linksys E1700 (or reverse-proxied one) and decode the command= value to read the injected shell command. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the device offline, and replace/firmware-update it — the vendor did not respond and the flaw is unpatched, so isolation is the only reliable fix. 3) Hunt: extract any payload URL/IP from the injected command and pivot on it across egress logs (UC2/UC3); sweep for the same source IP hitting other IoT endpoints.
union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | extend Uri = strcat(csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery), SrcIP = cIP, Host = Computer, Method = csMethod, Status = tostring(scStatus)),
  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | extend Uri = RequestURL, SrcIP = SourceIP, Host = DestinationHostName, Method = RequestMethod, Status = tostring(EventOutcome))
| where Uri has "/goform/systemCommand"
| where Uri has "command="
| where Uri has_any ("wget","curl","tftp","chmod","busybox",";","%3B","|","%7C","`","$(")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIP, Host, Method, Uri, Status
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IoT victim-relay node behavior (fan-in relay with UPnP NAT traversal) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the article's relay-only Dysphoria variant: a compromised device that accepts many inbound public connections and forwards them to a small set of upstream controllers, using UPnP to map ports through the local gateway. Surfaces hosts acting as botnet traffic relays rather than direct bots. Rationale: Targets the article's explicitly described 'victim relay' + UPnP-port-mapping design (relay-only build from June 25). The fan-in/thin-fan-out asymmetry is the observable signature of a device relaying bot traffic to hidden controllers; kept Low confidence/high FP because it depends on flow asymmetry and requires per-environment threshold tuning. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/dysphoria-iot-botnet-adds-blockchain-c2.html • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1090.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate P2P applications (BitTorrent, game servers, WebRTC) on a user device
  • Reverse proxy / load balancer or VPN concentrator inside the environment
  • CDN edge or caching node with high inbound fan-in
  • Home-office router with UPnP enabled hosting a legitimate service
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("PROXY","LB","VPN","CDN","CACHE")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is an IoT/edge device (not a sanctioned proxy/LB) and inspect the small set of upstream destinations — cross-check them against the distribution IPs (UC2). Look for UPnP AddPortMapping / SSDP (udp 1900) activity on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the device, disable UPnP on the gateway, and remove the mapped port forwards. 3) Hunt: pivot the identified upstream controller IPs across all egress logs to find sibling relays; check the device for weak-credential logons (UC4) and blockchain resolution (UC1) to confirm the Dysphoria chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize InboundSources = dcountif(RemoteIP, ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"),
            OutboundDests = dcountif(RemoteIP, ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionRequest")),
            Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 15)
    by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where InboundSources > 30 and OutboundDests between (1 .. 5)   // heavy fan-in, thin upstream = relay
| order by InboundSources desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| summarize InboundSources = dcountif(SrcIpAddr, NetworkDirection =~ "Inbound"),
            OutboundDests = dcountif(DstIpAddr, NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound"),
            Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber, 15)
    by DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where InboundSources > 30 and OutboundDests between (1 .. 5)
| order by InboundSources desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Machine account created by a non-privileged user (MachineAccountQuota abuse) — Certighost stepping stone · [LLM] AD CS Certification Authority (certsrv.exe) initiating SMB/LDAP to a non-DC host — Certighost chase redirect · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New Certighost PoC exploit lets attackers hijack Windows domains

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Machine account created by a non-privileged user (MachineAccountQuota abuse) — Certighost stepping stone AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the first Certighost step: a low-privileged domain user creating a computer/machine account via the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota, giving the attacker a valid domain principal to stand up the rogue chase endpoint. Surfaces the creator, the new machine account, and creation bursts. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit statement that the attacker 'first creates a machine account, which is permitted under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota configuration' — 4741 by a non-$ subject is the earliest observable. Cross-checked H0j3n gist and Dataminr/Help Net Security writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/27/certighost-cve-2026-54121-poc-exploit-released/
ATT&CKT1136.002 T1078.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/staff self-joining workstations via MachineAccountQuota (the same legitimate mechanism this abuses)
  • SCCM/MDT/autopilot provisioning running under a delegated non-tier0 account
  • Helpdesk staff with delegated computer-object create rights bulk-onboarding devices
  • Cluster/failover services registering CNO/VCO computer objects
  • Lab/test automation spinning up ephemeral machine accounts
Suppression filter
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("svc-sccm","svc-mdt","svc-autopilot") // append your approved provisioning identities
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether SubjectUserName is a known provisioning/service identity; if it's a standard user with no delegated join rights, treat as suspicious. Note the new machine account name for pivoting. 2) Contain: disable the newly created machine account and the creating user; consider setting ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 domain-wide. 3) Hunt: pivot on the new machine account name into UC2 (CA→non-DC connections), UC3 (PKINIT as a DC account), and UC5 (cert enrollment for a DC) within the following hours.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4741                              // A computer account was created
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"               // creator is a real user, not a tier-0 automation acct
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("SYSTEM","ANONYMOUS LOGON")
| summarize AccountsCreated = dcount(TargetUserName), NewMachineAccounts = make_set(TargetUserName, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName, Computer
| where AccountsCreated >= 1                          // any user-driven machine-account creation is worth review
| order by AccountsCreated desc
title: Machine Account Created by Non-Privileged User (Certighost precursor)

AD CS Certification Authority (certsrv.exe) initiating SMB/LDAP to a non-DC host — Certighost chase redirect AIExploitation High
Detects the core Certighost exploitation: the CA host's certificate service reaching out over SMB (445) / LDAP (389) / LDAPS (636) to an attacker-controlled 'cdc' endpoint that is not a legitimate domain controller. certsrv.exe egress to arbitrary internal hosts is highly abnormal. Rationale: Directly models the article's chase mechanism — 'the CA connects to the server specified in the cdc value' running 'rogue SMB, LSA, and LDAP services.' certsrv.exe only exists on CA servers, so scoping the initiating process to it makes CA→internal-host SMB/LDAP a low-FP, Certighost-specific signal. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/
ATT&CKT1649 T1187
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CA legitimately performing LDAP lookups against real domain controllers (exclude your DC subnets)
  • CA server also acting as a member server making SMB to file shares for CRL/AIA publication
  • Backup/monitoring agents co-resident on the CA generating SMB
  • CA cluster nodes talking to each other over SMB/LDAP
  • CES/CEP web-enrollment proxies performing directory reads
Suppression filter
| where RemoteDeviceName !in~ ("DC01","DC02") and ipv4_is_in_any_range(RemoteIP, "10.10.10.0/24") == false // replace with your DC hostnames / DC subnet
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve RemoteIP/RemoteDeviceName — is it a known domain controller? If it's a workstation, member server, or a recently created machine account host, treat as a Certighost chase. 2) Contain: isolate the destination host, revoke/hold pending certificate requests on the CA, and disable the EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC chase fallback (certutil -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC; Restart-Service CertSvc -Force) if July updates aren't yet applied. 3) Hunt: check the CA request queue for enrollments targeting DC accounts (UC5) and for subsequent PKINIT-as-DC (UC3) around the same timestamp.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "certsrv.exe"          // CA service host — only present on Enterprise CA servers
| where RemotePort in (445, 389, 636)                       // SMB / LDAP / LDAPS chase lookups
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize ConnCount = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 3
| where EventData has "certsrv.exe"
| extend Image = extract(@"<Data Name=""Image"">([^<]+)", 1, EventData),
         DestPort = toint(extract(@"<Data Name=""DestinationPort"">([0-9]+)", 1, EventData)),
         DestIp = extract(@"<Data Name=""DestinationIp"">([^<]+)", 1, EventData)
| where Image has "certsrv.exe"
| where DestPort in (445, 389, 636)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, DestIp, DestPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AD CS CertSrv Outbound SMB/LDAP to Internal Host (Certighost chase)

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app="certsrv.exe" (All_Traffic.dest_port=445 OR All_Traffic.dest_port=389 OR All_Traffic.dest_port=636) by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | sort - count

Certificate-based (PKINIT) Kerberos TGT requested for a computer/DC account — Certighost DC impersonation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the authentication payoff of Certighost: a Kerberos AS-REQ (4768) where a computer account ($) obtains a TGT via certificate-based PKINIT pre-authentication. Machine accounts authenticating with a certificate is rare and is exactly how the PoC impersonates the targeted domain controller. Rationale: Grounded on 'using the certificate to authenticate through PKINIT as the targeted domain controller.' A 4768 for a $ account carrying certificate info (PKINIT) is abnormal — normal machine TGTs use encrypted-timestamp pre-auth, not certificates. Defender left empty: DC-side KDC 4768 is not in endpoint AH tables (MDI surfaces it as an alert, not a raw huntable table). Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/
ATT&CKT1649 T1558
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Environments using certificate-based auth / smart-card logon for service or gMSA-style machine identities
  • Windows Hello for Business or device certificate enrollment scenarios that trigger PKINIT for computers
  • Legitimate AD CS auto-enrollment health checks
  • Third-party MDM/EDR agents authenticating machine identities via cert
  • Recently onboarded devices doing initial cert-based authentication
Suppression filter
| where TargetUserName !in~ ("WHFB-DEVICE$") // append machine identities you knowingly use cert/PKINIT auth for
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether TargetUserName is a domain controller computer account; if a DC account did cert-based PKINIT from an IpAddress that is not that DC's own address, escalate immediately. 2) Contain: revoke the issued certificate on the CA, reset the impacted DC computer account password (twice for krbtgt if DCSync followed), and isolate the source IP. 3) Hunt: immediately check UC4 (DS replication by that DC account within ~30 min) and pull the CA request that issued the cert (UC5).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4768                               // Kerberos TGT (AS-REQ) issued
| where TargetUserName endswith "$"                   // a computer/DC account requesting a TGT
| where EventData has "Certificate"                   // PKINIT: certificate-info section populated
| extend CertThumbprint = extract(@"Certificate Thumbprint(?:</Data>)?[^0-9A-Fa-f]*([0-9A-Fa-f]{20,})", 1, EventData)
| where isnotempty(CertThumbprint)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, TargetUserName, IpAddress, CertThumbprint
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PKINIT Certificate TGT for Computer Account (Certighost DC impersonation)

description: Detects a Kerberos AS-REQ (4768) where a computer account obtains a TGT via certificate-based PKINIT pre-authentication, the mechanism Certighost uses to authenticate as a targeted domain controller.

  cert:

  condition: selection and cert
level: high
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.signature_id=4768 Authentication.user="*$" by Authentication.user, Authentication.src, Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.signature_id=4768 Authentication.user="*$" by Authentication.user, Authentication.src, Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - firstTime
DCSync (DS-Replication-Get-Changes) immediately after PKINIT-as-DC — Certighost krbtgt theft AIActions on Objectives High
High-fidelity correlation of the Certighost end-game: a computer account performs certificate PKINIT (4768) and then, within a short window, invokes directory-replication rights (4662 GetNCChanges) — i.e. DCSync using the forged DC credential to pull secrets including krbtgt. Catches the case the classic 'exclude $ accounts' DCSync rule misses. Rationale: Models 'With the resulting Kerberos credential, the attacker can request account secrets, including the krbtgt secret.' Correlating cert-PKINIT-as-a-computer-account with the same account then exercising the replication extended rights (GUIDs 1131f6ad/1131f6aa) is Certighost-specific and sidesteps the standard DCSync rule that excludes machine accounts — precisely the account class Certighost impersonates. Cross-checked DCSync 4662 GUID detection guidance (Netero1010/NCC). Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.netero1010-securitylab.com/detection/dcsync-detection • https://www.nccgroup.com/research/defending-your-directory-an-expert-guide-to-securing-active-directory-against-dcsync-attacks/
ATT&CKT1003.006 T1649
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine DC-to-DC replication happening to fall near a machine cert auth (mitigated by requiring cert PKINIT + tight 30m window)
  • Azure AD Connect / MSOL sync accounts with replication rights (these are not $ machine accounts doing PKINIT)
  • Backup solutions using DRS replication under a service account
  • New DC promotion (dcpromo) generating legitimate replication bursts
  • Third-party AD auditing tools that request GetNCChanges
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Account is a DC computer account and that ReplDc/PkIp indicate the replication did not originate from that DC's own host — a delay of seconds-to-minutes after cert PKINIT is the Certighost signature. 2) Contain: reset krbtgt twice, reset the impacted DC computer account, revoke the issued certificate, and force-disable the chase fallback if unpatched. 3) Hunt: enumerate all objects the account replicated (ObjectName), assume krbtgt compromise → hunt for Golden Tickets and review all cert enrollments in the request queue (UC5).
IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "Directory Services replication"      // MDI DCSync telemetry
| project Timestamp, AccountName, AccountDomain, DeviceName, DeviceName, IPAddress, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
let win = 30m;
let pkinit = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4768 and TargetUserName endswith "$"
    | where EventData has "Certificate"                       // PKINIT cert pre-auth
    | project PkTime = TimeGenerated, Account = TargetUserName, PkIp = IpAddress, KdcHost = Computer;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4662 and ObjectServer == "DS"
| where EventData has_any ("1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2", "1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2", "89e95b76-444d-4c62-991a-0facbeda640c")  // DS-Replication-Get-Changes[-All / -In-Filtered-Set]
| project ReplTime = TimeGenerated, Account = SubjectUserName, ReplDc = Computer, ObjectName
| join kind=inner pkinit on Account
| where ReplTime between (PkTime .. PkTime + win)
| project PkTime, ReplTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', ReplTime, PkTime), Account, PkIp, KdcHost, ReplDc, ObjectName
| order by ReplTime desc

Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54121")

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
